teile.einleitung: Horseshoe crabs look like armoured helmets with a long spike as a tail. Despite their name they are not crabs at all, but are more closely related to spiders and scorpions. They have existed for hundreds of millions of years, and today their blue blood even helps medicine.
wichtigste: Horseshoe crabs belong to the chelicerates (Chelicerata), not to the crabs.
They form the order Xiphosura, and only four species are alive today.
Limulus polyphemus lives on the Atlantic coast of North America.
Their blood is blue because it contains copper-bearing haemocyanin.
The LAL test is made from the blood and detects endotoxins from bacteria.
The US authority FDA approved the LAL test in 1977.
The genetically engineered recombinant Factor C can replace the test.

abschnitte.text: A horseshoe crab has a horseshoe-shaped, hard **shell**, with its legs hidden underneath. At the back it has a long, pointed tail spine, which it uses to turn itself over when it is lying on its back. Females grow to about 60 centimetres including the spine and are larger than the males. On the shell sit two large **compound eyes** and several small eyes.

Although they are called crabs, horseshoe crabs belong to the **chelicerates** (Chelicerata) and are therefore related to spiders, scorpions and mites. They form the order Xiphosura. Their ancestors lived over 400 million years ago, which is why they are often called **living fossils**. Today only four species remain, one in North America and three in Asia.

The best-known species, **Limulus polyphemus**, lives on the Atlantic coast of North America and in the Gulf of Mexico. The three other species live on coasts of South and East Asia. Horseshoe crabs root around on the sea floor for worms, mussels and other small animals. In spring, at high tide, they come in their thousands to sandy beaches to lay their eggs, and Delaware Bay in the USA is especially well known.

The blood of horseshoe crabs is blue because it contains the copper-bearing pigment **haemocyanin**, whereas our blood is red because of iron-bearing haemoglobin. In the 1950s the researcher Frederik Bang discovered at Woods Hole that their blood clots when bacteria are present. From this came the **LAL test**, the abbreviation standing for Limulus amoebocyte lysate. The test detects endotoxins of gram-negative bacteria, that is, poisonous substances that can cause fever.

The LAL test is used to check whether vaccines, syringes and medicines are free of dangerous bacterial toxins. The US medicines authority FDA approved it in 1977, and it largely replaced the pyrogen test on **rabbits**. For the test, blood is taken from captured animals, and afterwards they are returned to the sea, but some of them do not survive. At the National University of Singapore, the researcher Jeak Ling Ding developed **recombinant Factor C**, a genetically engineered alternative that uses no animal blood.

Horseshoe crabs have come under pressure from blood collection, fishing for use as bait and the loss of beaches. Their eggs are important food for migratory birds such as the **red knot**, which stops off at Delaware Bay on its long flight to the Arctic. If the crabs decline, the birds therefore suffer too. Today there are catch rules and protected areas, and more and more companies are relying on the artificial substitute test.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals including spiders, scorpions and mites, whose first mouthparts are small claws.
A blue, copper-bearing blood pigment that carries oxygen.
A poisonous substance from the wall of certain bacteria that can cause fever.
A living thing that has hardly changed for a very long time.

gewusst: Horseshoe crabs existed long before the dinosaurs.
A litre of horseshoe crab blood is very valuable and can cost thousands of dollars.
Almost everyone who has had a vaccination was probably protected by a test using horseshoe crab blood.

teile.einleitung: Panthera is the scientific name of the genus of big cats. It includes the lion, the tiger, the leopard, the jaguar and the snow leopard. They are the largest and strongest cats in the world, and most of them can roar.
wichtigste: Panthera is the genus of big cats.
It includes the lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard.
Lions, tigers and leopards live in Africa and Asia, the jaguar in the Americas.
Most Panthera species can roar.
The tiger is the largest cat in the world.
All five species are considered threatened or near threatened.

abschnitte.text: **Panthera** is a genus within the cat family. These animals are called **big cats** together. Today the genus includes five species: lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard. All of them are predators that can hunt large prey such as deer, antelopes or wild boar.

The **lion** lives mainly in the savannas of Africa, with a small group also in India. The tiger is found only in Asia, from India to the east of Russia. The leopard is the most widespread and lives in Africa and Asia. The **jaguar** is the only Panthera species in the Americas, and the snow leopard lives in the high mountains of Central Asia.

Big cats have a powerful body, strong jaws and long canine teeth. Most of them can **roar** loudly because their larynx is built in a special way. In return, unlike house cats, they cannot purr continuously. The snow leopard is an exception: it cannot roar.

The **tiger** is the largest cat in the world, and large male Siberian tigers can weigh over 250 kilograms. The lion is hardly smaller and is the only cat that lives in prides. In proportion to its size, the jaguar has the strongest bite of all cats. The snow leopard uses its very long tail as a balancing aid and as a scarf against the cold.

The ancestors of the big cats appeared several million years ago, probably in Asia. During the ice ages the **cave lion**, a close relative of today's lion, lived in Europe. Remains of such animals have also been found in caves in Europe, and people of the Stone Age painted them on cave walls. Today there are no wild big cats left in Europe.

All big cats are threatened by **poaching**, the destruction of their habitat and conflicts with people. Only a few thousand tigers are left in the wild. Many protected areas and programmes aim to save the big cats. In Swiss zoos such as Zurich and Basel you can see big cats that take part in breeding programmes to protect their species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related animal species.
Another name for the large cats of the genus Panthera.
The organ in the throat that produces sounds.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.

gewusst: The clouded leopard looks like a big cat but belongs to a genus of its own.
A lion's roar can be heard several kilometres away.
Black panthers are not a separate species either, but dark leopards or jaguars.

teile.einleitung: “Peter and the Wolf” is a famous musical fairy tale for children by the Russian composer Sergei Prokofiev. A narrator tells the story, and each character is played by an instrument of its own. In this exciting way, children get to know the instruments of an orchestra.
wichtigste: “Peter and the Wolf” was composed in 1936 by Sergei Prokofiev.
It is a fairy tale for narrator and orchestra.
Each character has its own instrument and its own melody.
The wolf is represented by three horns.
Peter catches the wolf with a rope, and the hunters take it to the zoo.
The piece lasts about half an hour.
It is still performed all over the world today.

abschnitte.text: The Russian composer **Sergei Prokofiev** lived from 1891 to 1953. He wrote “Peter and the Wolf” in 1936 in Moscow for a children's theatre. He wrote not only the music but also the text of the story himself. The aim was to bring the instruments of the orchestra closer to children.

The boy Peter lives with his grandfather at the edge of a forest. One day a wolf slinks out of the forest and swallows the duck. Peter bravely climbs a tree and, with the help of the little bird and a **rope**, catches the wolf by the tail. The hunters arrive, and everyone takes the wolf to the zoo in a triumphal procession.

Each character has its own instrument and its own **theme**, that is, a melody you can recognise. Peter is played by the string instruments, the bird by the flute and the duck by the **oboe**. The cat creeps along with the clarinet, and the grandfather grumbles with the bassoon. The wolf is played by three horns, and the hunters' shots can be heard on the timpani.

At the start, the narrator introduces each character with its instrument. In this way, as you listen, you can tell who is currently appearing in the story. When the wolf appears, the music sounds dark and threatening. At the end you can even hear the duck quacking softly in the wolf's belly, because in his haste the wolf swallowed it whole.

“Peter and the Wolf” is one of the best-known works of **classical music** for children. Many famous people have taken on the narrator's role, in the German-speaking world for example the humorist Loriot. There are animated films, for example one by Walt Disney from 1946. A puppet animation from 2006 even won an **Oscar**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who invents and writes down music.
A large group of musicians with many different instruments.
A short melody that you can recognise again and again.
The person who reads out the story between the pieces of music.

gewusst: Prokofiev is said to have written the music for “Peter and the Wolf” in just a few days.
Prokofiev died on the same day as the Soviet ruler Joseph Stalin.
In many Swiss schools and concert halls there are family concerts with “Peter and the Wolf”.

teile.einleitung: Phoresy means that one animal lets itself be transported by another animal without harming it. It is like hitchhiking in the animal world. Small animals such as mites in particular use this trick to reach new habitats.
wichtigste: Phoresy is the transport of one animal by another without harming it.
The word comes from Greek and means “carrying”.
It is usually small, slow animals that let themselves be carried.
Some mites let dung beetles carry them to fresh dung.
Pseudoscorpions also often travel on flies or beetles.
The transporting animal is not eaten and not sucked dry.

abschnitte.text: In **phoresy**, one animal clings to another and lets itself be taken along. The word comes from the Greek “phoresis”, which means “carrying”. The passenger uses the transporting animal only as a vehicle and does not feed on it. This is what distinguishes phoresy from **parasitism**, in which one animal harms another.

A well-known example is **mites** on dung beetles and burying beetles. Dung and animal carcasses are only there for a short time and lie far apart. The tiny mites could hardly reach these food sources on foot. So they climb onto a beetle and get off again at the next pile of dung or carcass.

**Pseudoscorpions** are tiny arachnids with pincers that often live under bark or in leaf litter. To get further away, they grab the leg of a fly or beetle with their pincers and fly along. Some roundworms also travel on insects to new habitats. In oil beetles, the young larvae climb onto wild bees and let themselves be carried into their nests.

The **remora** is a fish that attaches itself with a sucker on its head to sharks, whales or turtles. In this way it saves energy and eats scraps from its carrier's prey. Because it also feeds, this relationship is usually counted as **commensalism**, a related form of living together. The boundaries between phoresy and other forms are not always sharp.

Phoresy helps small animals to spread far and to settle new habitats. Sometimes even the carrier gains an advantage: mites on burying beetles, for example, eat fly eggs on the carcass and so protect the food of the beetle larvae. In a similar way, plants spread seeds with hooks in the fur of animals, as the burdock does. Researchers study phoresy to understand better how living things are connected.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal lets itself be transported by another without harming it.
A way of living together in which one animal exploits and harms another.
A way of living together in which one gains and the other has neither benefit nor harm.
A tiny arachnid with pincers but without a venomous sting.

gewusst: Some mites wait motionless on flowers until a hummingbird comes by, and then dash into its bill to fly along to the next flower.
Pseudoscorpions are often only a few millimetres in size and completely harmless to people.
Dozens of mites can ride along on a single burying beetle at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The paw is the foot of many mammals such as dogs, cats, foxes or bears. Under the paw lie soft pads, the paw pads, which work like shock absorbers. Paws also have claws, with which the animals dig, climb or hunt.
wichtigste: Paws are the feet of many mammals, for example dogs and cats.
The soft cushions under the paws are called pads.
Dogs sweat mainly through the pads of their paws.
Cats can draw in their claws, dogs cannot.
Dogs and cats walk on their toes, so they are digitigrade.
In hunters' language, the print of a paw is called a track.

abschnitte.text: A paw consists of the toes with their **claws** and several soft cushions, the **pads**. In dogs and cats there is a small toe pad under each toe and, behind them, a large main pad. The pads have thick, rough skin and a layer of fat underneath. In this way they cushion the shocks when running and jumping.

Dogs and cats are **digitigrade**: they walk only on their toes, and the heel does not touch the ground. This makes them fast and quiet. Bears, by contrast, are **plantigrade** and put the whole sole of the foot down, much as we humans do. Dogs and cats usually have five toes at the front and four at the back, with the inner front toe sitting higher up and not touching the ground.

Cats can draw their pointed claws into sheaths of skin, so that they stay sharp and the cat creeps along silently. When climbing or hunting, it extends the claws in a flash. Dogs cannot draw in their claws, which is why you can hear them clicking on hard floors. They use their claws mainly for **digging** and for a good grip when running.

Dogs and cats have hardly any sweat glands in their skin. They sweat mainly through the **paw pads**, which is why on hot days they sometimes leave damp prints. To cool down, dogs mostly pant. The pads are also very sensitive and feel the ground, warmth and vibrations.

Animals from cold regions have special paws: the polar bear and the Arctic fox have fur on their soles, which keeps them warm and stops them slipping. The lynx has broad, hairy paws that work like **snowshoes** in deep snow. For dogs in Switzerland, road salt in winter and hot asphalt in summer are a danger to the pads. Dog owners therefore care for the paws with grease or rinse them off after a walk.

In hunters' language, the print of a paw is called a **track**. From the tracks in snow or mud you can tell which animal has passed by. In a dog's print you can usually see the claws, but not in a cat's, because it draws its claws in. A fox track is narrower than a dog track, and the fox often places its paws in a dead straight line one behind the other.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft, thick cushion under the paw.
A hard, pointed nail on an animal's toe.
An animal that walks only on its toes, like a dog and a cat.
The print of a paw in the ground.

gewusst: The paw pads of some dogs smell slightly of popcorn, because of bacteria on the skin.
Cats have scent glands in their paws and mark their territory when scratching.
Many dogs and cats prefer one paw, much as people are right-handed or left-handed.

teile.einleitung: The Indian rhinoceros is a large rhinoceros from Asia whose thick skin lies in folds and looks like a knight's armour. It lives in India and Nepal and has just a single horn on its nose. A good hundred years ago it was almost extinct, but thanks to protection measures there are again several thousand animals today.
wichtigste: The Indian rhinoceros lives in Asia, mainly in India and Nepal.
It has only one horn.
Its skin lies in thick folds that look like armour plating.
After the white rhinoceros, it is one of the largest rhinoceros species.
Indian rhinoceroses eat grasses and water plants and are good swimmers.
Today about 4,000 Indian rhinoceroses live in the wild again (as of 2022).
In 1956 the first Indian rhinoceros ever born in a zoo came into the world at Basel Zoo.

abschnitte.text: The Indian rhinoceros is called **Rhinoceros unicornis** in science, which means one-horned rhinoceros. Its grey skin is very thick and lies in deep **skin folds** that look like the plates of a suit of armour. Males can weigh over 2 tonnes. The single **horn** is made of keratin, the same substance as our fingernails, and is usually 20 to 30 centimetres long.

Indian rhinoceroses live in the north of India and the south of Nepal. They like damp **floodplains** with tall grass, swamps and rivers at the foot of the Himalayas. The most animals live in Kaziranga National Park in the Indian state of Assam, which is home to about two thirds of all Indian rhinoceroses. Another important protected area is Chitwan National Park in Nepal.

The Indian rhinoceros is a **herbivore** and eats mainly tall grasses, but also leaves, fruit and water plants. It likes to wallow in mud and bathes in water for hours to cool down. It is also a good swimmer and can even dive. The animals mostly live alone, and only mothers stay with their young for a few years.

A female is pregnant for about 16 months and then gives birth to a single calf. The young one already weighs about 60 kilograms at birth. It stays with its mother for around two to three years. Indian rhinoceroses can live to 40 years and older.

Around 1900 only about 200 Indian rhinoceroses were left, because they had been hunted and their habitat destroyed. Thanks to strictly protected areas and rangers, the population grew again to about 4,000 animals (as of 2022). The greatest danger remains **poaching**, because in some countries people wrongly believe that the horn is a medicine. The Indian rhinoceros is now considered vulnerable, but no longer endangered with extinction.

**Basel Zoo** is known worldwide for its Indian rhinoceroses. In 1956 the first Indian rhinoceros ever born in a zoo came into the world there. Since then many more young animals have grown up in Basel, and some were passed on to other zoos. The zoo takes part in the **breeding programme** that aims to preserve the species in human care.

begriffe.erklaerung: The horn-like substance that rhinoceros horns, hair and fingernails are made of.
Places where the thick skin lies in layers on top of each other.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.
Rolling in mud to cool down and to protect against insects.

gewusst: In 1515 the artist Albrecht Dürer made a famous woodcut of an Indian rhinoceros without ever having seen one.
Indian rhinoceroses use shared dung sites, which work like signposts for other rhinoceroses.
Despite its weight, an Indian rhinoceros can run at over 40 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: The Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland on Earth and lies in the heart of South America. Most of it belongs to Brazil, with smaller parts in Bolivia and Paraguay. Here live more jaguars, caimans and waterbirds than almost anywhere else.
wichtigste: The Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland in the world.
Most of it lies in Brazil.
In the rainy season, a large part of the area is flooded.
Particularly many jaguars live in the Pantanal.
Other typical animals are capybaras, spectacled caimans and hyacinth macaws.
Part of the Pantanal has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 2000.
Fires and drought threaten the area.

abschnitte.text: The Pantanal lies in the west of **Brazil**, in the states of Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul. Smaller parts belong to Bolivia and Paraguay. It covers around 150,000 square kilometres, which is more than three times the size of Switzerland. The **Paraguay River** flows through the area with many tributaries.

The name Pantanal comes from the Portuguese word pântano, which means swamp. In the **rainy season**, from about November to March, the rivers burst their banks and flood large parts of the plain. In the dry season the water withdraws, leaving lagoons and pools. Many animals then gather at the last watering places, which makes them easy to watch.

One of the densest **jaguar** populations in the world lives in the Pantanal. The jaguars here are especially large and good swimmers, and they even hunt caimans in the water. Other typical animals are the **capybara**, the largest rodent in the world, the spectacled caiman, the giant otter and the marsh deer. In the sky you can see the blue hyacinth macaw and the jabiru, a large stork.

Only a few people live in the Pantanal, and most of the land belongs to large farms. For centuries people here have kept **cattle**, which graze on the grasslands in the dry season. The cattle herders are called Pantaneiros. **Ecotourism** is becoming more and more important, because many travellers come to watch jaguars and other animals.

In 2020, after an extreme drought, huge areas of the Pantanal burned down and many animals died. New fields, dams and waterways also change the natural water balance. In 2000 part of the area was named a **UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site**. Conservation organisations work with farmers so that jaguars and cattle can live side by side.

begriffe.erklaerung: A landscape that is often or permanently under water, such as swamps and bogs.
The time of year with a great deal of rain in tropical regions.
Travel into nature that is as gentle as possible on the environment and the local people.
A particularly valuable natural area that has been recognised by UNESCO.

gewusst: Millions of spectacled caimans live in the Pantanal.
Pantanal jaguars often kill caimans with a single bite to the head.
A capybara can grow as heavy as a grown-up person.

teile.einleitung: The pelagic zone is the area of open water in a lake or sea, far from the shore and not on the bottom. Here, for example, the whitefish swim in our Swiss lakes. In the sea, the pelagic zone is the largest habitat on the whole Earth.
wichtigste: The pelagic zone is the open-water zone of a body of water.
It lies away from the shore and above the bottom of the water.
The bottom area is called the benthic zone, the shore area the littoral zone.
Plankton and free-swimming animals such as fish live in the pelagic zone.
In Swiss lakes, whitefish mostly swim in open water.
In the sea, the pelagic zone is divided into several zones according to depth.

abschnitte.text: The word pelagic comes from the Greek word “pelagos”, which means “open sea”. It refers to all the water that is not directly at the shore and not at the bottom. The bottom of a body of water is called the **benthic zone**, the shore area the **littoral zone**. The pelagic zone is therefore like a huge, freely floating body of water.

In the sea, the pelagic zone is divided by depth. The top layer, down to about 200 metres, is called the **epipelagic zone**, and there is enough light there for plants. Below it follow the mesopelagic zone down to about 1,000 metres, the pitch-dark bathypelagic zone and, deeper still, the abyssopelagic zone. The deeper you go, the colder and darker it gets, and the water pressure rises sharply.

Two large groups of living things live in the pelagic zone. **Plankton** drifts with the current, and includes tiny algae and small animals such as water fleas. **Nekton** are animals that can actively swim against the current, for example fish, squid and whales. Many animals in the open sea are silvery or transparent, so that they are hard to see.

abschnitte.titel: The pelagic zone in Swiss lakes
abschnitte.text: In large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Geneva or Lake Lucerne there is an extensive pelagic zone. This is where the **whitefish** live, which feed on plankton. Arctic char and lake trout also often hunt in open water. Fishers therefore use floating nets in open water to catch whitefish.

In the upper, bright layer, tiny algae grow that make food using sunlight. They are the start of the **food chain** in open water. Small animals eat the algae, fish eat the small animals, and larger predators eat the fish. Dead living things sink slowly into the depths and feed other animals there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The open-water zone of a lake or sea, away from the shore and the bottom.
The habitat at the bottom of a body of water.
The shore area of a body of water, where light reaches the bottom.
All animals that can swim independently in water, such as fish.

gewusst: By volume, the pelagic zone of the oceans is the largest habitat on our planet.
Many animals from the depths rise to the top every night to feed and dive down again in the morning.
Some deep-sea animals in the dark pelagic zone make light themselves.

teile.einleitung: Parthenogenesis, also called virgin birth, is reproduction without fertilisation. A new living thing develops from an unfertilised egg cell, with no male at all. In aphids this happens very often in summer.
wichtigste: Parthenogenesis means virgin birth.
In it, an offspring arises from an unfertilised egg cell.
Aphids often multiply by parthenogenesis in summer.
In honeybees, the males, the drones, develop from unfertilised eggs.
Water fleas, stick insects and some lizards can also reproduce this way.
The Geneva naturalist Charles Bonnet observed virgin birth in aphids in the 18th century.
In mammals, parthenogenesis does not occur in nature.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek: parthenos means virgin and genesis means origin. Normally in reproduction an **egg cell** and a sperm cell fuse. In **parthenogenesis**, however, the egg cell goes on developing without fertilisation. The offspring therefore have only the mother's genes and are often very similar to her.

**Aphids** are the best-known examples of virgin birth. In spring and summer the females give birth to live daughters without any males, and these sometimes already carry the next generation inside them. In this way huge colonies build up in a short time on roses or beans. Only in autumn do males appear again, and the females lay fertilised eggs that survive the winter.

In the **honeybee**, the queen decides whether an egg is fertilised. Fertilised eggs become females, that is, workers or queens. Unfertilised eggs hatch into the males, which are called **drones**. Many stick insects and water fleas also reproduce wholly or at times without males.

Among some lizards there are species made up only of females, for example certain whiptail lizards in North America and rock lizards in the Caucasus. In 2006, Komodo dragons in two English zoos had offspring even though they had never had contact with a male. Virgin birth has also been observed in sharks in aquariums and in some snakes. In **mammals** it does not occur in nature.

Around 1740 the Geneva naturalist **Charles Bonnet** raised a single aphid completely shielded from others. It still had many young, and so Bonnet recognised virgin birth. His observation was a sensation in science at the time. He is therefore regarded as one of the discoverers of parthenogenesis.

The great advantage is that the animals can multiply very quickly, because every animal has offspring. A single female can even found a new colony on her own. The disadvantage is that the genes hardly mix and the offspring are very similar. As a result, they are less able to **adapt** to new diseases or changes in the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for parthenogenesis, reproduction without fertilisation.
The female reproductive cell from which a new living thing can develop.
The fusing of an egg cell and a sperm cell.
A male honeybee.

gewusst: In aphids, a baby can already carry its own daughters inside it while still in its mother's body.
Some species of whiptail lizards are made up only of females.
A drone has a mother but no father.

teile.einleitung: Baboons are large, strong monkeys that live mainly in Africa. Because of their long, dog-like muzzle they are also called dog-faced monkeys. They live in large groups and are very clever.
wichtigste: Baboons make up the genus Papio and belong to the Old World monkeys.
Most baboon species live in Africa, and one species also on the Arabian Peninsula.
Because of their long muzzle they are also called dog-faced monkeys.
Baboons spend most of the day on the ground.
They live in groups with several males and many females with young.
A female usually has only one young at a time.
In the wild, baboons live to about 20 to 30 years.

abschnitte.text: Baboons have a strong body, long arms and legs and a long, dog-like **muzzle**. The males are clearly larger than the females and have long, sharp **canine teeth**. On the rump, baboons have bare, hardened sitting pads, on which they can sit comfortably. In females, the skin on the rump swells and turns red around ovulation, which shows the males that they are ready to mate.

Baboons live in savannas, steppes, semi-deserts and rocky mountains. Well-known species include the **olive baboon**, the chacma baboon, the yellow baboon, the Guinea baboon and the **hamadryas baboon**. The hamadryas baboon lives in north-east Africa and on the Arabian Peninsula, and the males wear a silvery-grey mane like a cloak. Where it is dry, baboons dig for water in dried-up riverbeds.

Baboons are **omnivores** and not fussy. They eat grasses, roots, seeds, fruit and tubers, but also insects, eggs and sometimes small animals. With their skilful hands they dig food out of the ground. If they live near settlements, they get used to human food and sometimes raid rubbish bins, fields or even cars.

Most baboon species live in groups called **troops**, with several males and many females with their young. In the group there is a clear pecking order. The animals groom each other's fur, which is called **grooming** or picking lice, and it strengthens friendships. If an enemy such as a leopard appears, the group defends itself together, especially the strong males.

A female baboon is pregnant for about six months and usually has a single young. The newborn has dark fur and at first clings to its mother's belly. Later it rides along on her back, like a little jockey. Only after several years is a young baboon fully grown.

In ancient Egypt the hamadryas baboon was regarded as a sacred animal of the god **Thoth**, the god of wisdom and writing. Today baboons live in many zoos, including in Europe. In Africa they sometimes come into conflict with farmers because they raid fields. Most baboon species are currently not considered seriously threatened, but in some places they are losing their habitat.

begriffe.erklaerung: Monkeys from Africa and Asia whose nostrils lie close together and point downwards.
Thick, hard cushions of skin on the rump on which baboons sit.
The name for a group of baboons that lives and moves around together.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.

gewusst: Baboons communicate with barks, grunts and screams, but also with gestures such as yawning, which shows their large canine teeth.
A male baboon can grow twice as heavy as a female.
At night baboons like to sleep on rocks or tall trees, where they are safe from predators.

teile.einleitung: Poison dart frogs are small, often brightly coloured frogs from the rainforests of Central and South America. Their bright colours warn enemies: many species have a strong poison in their skin. The golden poison frog is even one of the most poisonous animals in the world.
wichtigste: Poison dart frogs form the family Dendrobatidae with around 200 species.
Their sister group is the family Aromobatidae.
The genus name Dendrobates means “tree walker”.
Indigenous hunters coated blowpipe darts with the skin poison, which is where the name comes from.
It is proven that only species of the genus Phyllobates were used for this.
The golden poison frog lives only in Colombia and contains batrachotoxin.
The bright colours warn enemies about the poison.

abschnitte.text: Most poison dart frogs are small, many only 1.5 to 5 centimetres long. They glow red, yellow, blue, green or orange, often with black spots. These bright **warning colours** tell birds and snakes: watch out, I am poisonous! The genus name Dendrobates means “tree walker”, although many species also live on the forest floor.

Poison dart frogs live in tropical **rainforests** from Nicaragua to Bolivia and Brazil. The family Dendrobatidae now includes around 200 species, and its closest relative is the family Aromobatidae. The **golden poison frog** (Phyllobates terribilis) lives only in Colombia, on the Pacific coast. Its range is smaller than 5,000 square kilometres and lies from sea level up to about 200 metres in height.

The golden poison frog grows to about 5 centimetres and is bright yellow. Its skin poison is called **batrachotoxin** and paralyses nerves and muscles. Even the amount in a single frog could kill several people, which is why its species name “terribilis” means terrible. The frogs do not make the poison themselves but take it in with their food, mainly through ants and mites.

Indigenous hunters in Colombia coated the tips of their **blowpipe darts** with the frogs' skin poison. In this way they could bring down birds and monkeys. It is proven that only species of the genus **Phyllobates** were used for this, even though all species of the family carry the name. Many other poison dart frogs are only weakly poisonous.

Poison dart frogs look after their young remarkably well. The eggs are laid on land in damp leaves and guarded by one of the parents. After hatching, the male often carries the **tadpoles** on his back to small pools of water, for example in the leaf axils of bromeliads. In some species the female even feeds the tadpoles with unfertilised eggs.

Many poison dart frogs are threatened because rainforest is being cut down. A dangerous **fungal disease** is also affecting amphibians worldwide. In the past many animals were caught for the pet trade, but today the trade is strictly regulated. Incidentally, poison dart frogs bred in zoos and terrariums are not poisonous, because they lack the poisonous food.

begriffe.erklaerung: A striking colour that shows enemies that an animal is poisonous or inedible.
A very strong nerve poison from the skin of some poison dart frogs.
A long tube through which small darts are shot with the breath.
The larva of a frog, which lives in water and breathes with gills.

gewusst: Poison dart frogs bred in captivity lose their poison because they eat different insects.
Poison dart frogs are active by day, while many other frogs are out at night.
A species of snake in South America can withstand the poison of some poison dart frogs and still eats them.

teile.einleitung: Horses come in many different colours, and each colour has its own name. A black horse is called a black, a reddish-brown one a chestnut and a white one a grey. Anyone who knows these names can describe horses the way experts do.
wichtigste: A black horse is simply called black.
A horse with reddish-brown fur is called a chestnut.
A white or light grey horse is called a grey.
A bay has brown fur with a black mane and a black tail.
Greys are usually born dark and only turn light over the years.
White markings on the head and legs are called markings.

abschnitte.text: The three basic colours in horses are **black**, **chestnut** and **bay**. A black horse is completely black, with a black mane and a black tail. A chestnut has reddish-brown fur, and its mane is the same colour or lighter. A bay has brown fur but a black mane, a black tail and usually dark legs.

A **grey** looks white or light grey. Most greys are born dark and only get lighter and lighter over the years. The Lipizzaners are well known for this, as their foals are born black or brown. In between, young greys often have a spotted coat, which is called dapple grey.

A **dun** has a sand-coloured or greyish-brown coat and often a dark stripe along the back, the dorsal stripe. A palomino is golden yellow with a light, almost white mane. Horses with large white and coloured patches are called **pintos**. Leopard-spotted horses have many small dark spots on a light coat, as seen in Appaloosas.

White areas on the head and legs are called **markings**. A small white patch on the forehead is called a star, and a long white stripe down the face is called a blaze. A white patch between the nostrils is called a snip. Markings help to identify a horse unmistakably, which is why they are also written in the horse passport.

The colour a horse has is determined by its **genes**, which it inherits from its mother and father. Some breeds are almost always the same colour: Friesians are black, and Haflingers are chestnuts with a light mane. Swiss Franches-Montagnes are mostly bays or chestnuts. In other breeds, such as the Icelandic horse, by contrast, a great many colours occur.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horse with black fur, a black mane and a black tail.
A horse with reddish-brown fur.
A horse with white or light grey fur.
White areas on a horse's head or legs.

gewusst: A grey is usually not white from birth, but only turns light with time.
Under the white coat of a grey, the skin is mostly dark.
The German word “Fuchs” for a chestnut horse comes from the reddish colour that is reminiscent of a red fox.

teile.einleitung: PanEco is a Swiss foundation that works to protect orangutans and their habitat. It was founded in the 1990s by the biologist Regina Frey and is based in Berg am Irchel in the canton of Zurich. It is also active in protecting nature in Switzerland.
wichtigste: PanEco is a nature conservation foundation from Switzerland.
It was founded by the biologist Regina Frey.
Its headquarters are in Berg am Irchel in the canton of Zurich.
PanEco works for orangutans in Indonesia, especially on Sumatra.
The foundation rescues orphaned orangutans and prepares them for life in the forest.
In Switzerland, PanEco runs the Thurauen Nature Centre in the Zurich Weinland.

abschnitte.text: PanEco is a non-profit **foundation** that was founded about 30 years ago by the Swiss biologist Regina Frey. As early as the 1970s, Regina Frey was working with orangutans in Indonesia. The foundation is based in Berg am Irchel in the canton of Zurich. It works in Indonesia and in Switzerland and combines species protection with environmental education.

In the wild, orangutans now live only on the islands of **Borneo** and Sumatra. PanEco works for these seriously threatened great apes, with its main focus on **Sumatra**. Together with Indonesian partners, the foundation runs a station where injured or orphaned orangutans are cared for. There, young animals learn to climb and find food before they are released into protected forests.

Orangutans can only survive if their **rainforest** is preserved. The greatest danger is deforestation, for example to make way for oil palm plantations. That is why PanEco also works to have forests placed under protection and to replant areas that have been destroyed. The foundation also supports farming families on the spot in using nature-friendly farming methods.

In Switzerland, PanEco runs the **Thurauen Nature Centre** near Flaach in the Zurich Weinland. There the River Thur was restored to a more natural state, so that a **floodplain landscape** rich in species could develop. Visitors can discover beavers, kingfishers and dragonflies on an adventure trail. The foundation also includes a bird of prey station in Berg am Irchel, which cares for injured birds of prey.

PanEco offers materials for school classes and organises guided tours and excursions. Children and young people learn how the rainforest and Swiss nature are connected. One example is our own shopping: anyone who chooses products with sustainable **palm oil** is helping the orangutans. Many people also support the foundation with donations or sponsorships.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that uses donated money to pursue a particular good cause.
Letting an animal that has been in human care go back into nature.
A natural landscape along a river that is flooded regularly.
The group of apes that includes orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos.

gewusst: Young orangutans stay with their mother for about seven to eight years, longer than almost any other animal.
The word orangutan comes from Malay and means forest person.
A Swiss foundation helps great apes on the other side of the world and, at the same time, beavers in the canton of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: The horse is one of the most important domestic animals for humans. For thousands of years horses have carried riders, pulled carts and ploughs and been faithful companions. Horses are fast, clever animals of flight that live in herds.
wichtigste: Horses live in groups called herds.
A wild herd of horses is often led by an older, experienced mare.
Horses eat mainly grass and hay, preferably in many small portions.
A horse has only one toe on each foot, the hoof.
A mare carries her foal in her belly for about 11 months.
Horses live to be about 25 to 30 years old.
Horses can breathe only through the nose.

abschnitte.text: A horse stands on four long legs, and on each foot it has only one toe, protected by a hard **hoof**. Its size is measured as the **height at the withers**, from the ground to the withers, the highest point of the back. The nostrils are especially large so that the horse can breathe in plenty of air when running. Because its throat is built the way it is, a horse can breathe only through its nose and not through its mouth.

Horses are herbivores and eat mostly **grass and hay**. In nature they eat for up to 16 hours a day, in small portions again and again. For this they have large molar teeth, which wear down and keep growing. A horse cannot vomit, so spoiled food or wrong feeding can cause dangerous **colic**.

Horses are **animals of flight**: when in danger, they would rather run away than fight. With their eyes set at the sides, they can see almost all the way round. In a wild herd an older, experienced mare often leads the group to food and water. In a stable, horses need contact with other horses and enough exercise, otherwise they become unhappy.

A female horse is called a mare, a male a stallion and a young one a **foal**. The mare carries her foal in her belly for about 11 months. Shortly after birth the foal can already stand and run, so that it can keep up with the herd. It drinks its mother's milk for several months.

Horses move in three basic gaits: **walk, trot and canter**. At a gallop, racehorses reach over 60 kilometres per hour. When a horse exerts itself hard, it sweats all over its body, a bit like a person. Horses can even doze while standing, because their legs can lock into place as if with a latch.

Humans tamed the horse a few thousand years ago in the steppes of Eurasia. After that, horses changed farming, trade and warfare. The best-known Swiss horse breed is the **Franches-Montagnes** from the Jura, a versatile, calm horse. In Avenches in the canton of Vaud there is the Swiss National Stud Farm, and today horses are kept mainly for sport and leisure.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard horny shoe at the end of each horse's leg.
A female horse.
A young horse.
An animal that runs away when in danger instead of fighting.
The size of a horse, measured from the ground to the withers.

gewusst: A horse's eyes are among the largest of all land mammals.
Horses can sleep standing up, but they lie down for deep sleep.
Experts can estimate a horse's age from its teeth.

teile.einleitung: Pacing is a gait in which an animal moves both legs on one side of its body forward at the same time. Camels and giraffes walk like this, and as they do they sway from one side to the other. Some horse breeds, such as the Icelandic horse, also master a special form of pacing.
wichtigste: In pacing, both legs on one side of the body move at the same time.
Camels walk with a pacing gait.
Giraffes and some bears also use this gait.
In pacing, the body sways from side to side.
Pacing is the counterpart of the trot, in which diagonal legs move together.
Icelandic horses can do the fast flying pace.

abschnitte.text: In **pacing**, both left legs first start moving at the same time and then both right legs. The body is therefore carried alternately on the left and on the right side. That is why an animal pacing sways like a boat. Camels are therefore also called ships of the desert.

Most four-legged animals, such as dogs, horses or cows, move to a different beat. In the **trot**, the legs move crosswise, so the left front leg moves together with the right hind leg. This gait is also called the **diagonal gait**. It is very stable, because the animal always stands on diagonally opposite legs.

Besides the **camel**, giraffes also pace when walking slowly. Some bears, elephants and a few dogs, especially when tired, also show pace-like movements. In animals with long legs, pacing has an advantage, because the front and hind legs do not knock into each other. This gait also saves energy when an animal covers long distances.

Some horse breeds can pace naturally, and they are called **gaited horses**. The best known is the **Icelandic horse**, which besides walk, trot and canter can also do the tölt and the fast flying pace. Icelandic horses are very popular in Switzerland too, and there are many farms and competitions for them here. In North America, in some harness races, horses even run at the pace instead of the trot.

In the Middle Ages, horses with a pacing gait were highly valued because they were comfortable to ride. Travellers, merchants and fine ladies therefore liked to ride on so-called **palfreys**. As better roads and carriages were built, these horses were needed less. In Iceland, however, the tradition has survived to this day, because for a long time there were hardly any roads there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way an animal moves its legs when it moves along.
A gait in which both legs on one side of the body move forward together.
A gait in which diagonally opposite legs move together.
A particularly comfortable gait of Icelandic horses with no moment of suspension.

gewusst: Camels are called ships of the desert because of their swaying pace, and some riders even get seasick from it.
A flying pace in Icelandic horses can be as fast as a canter.
In the Middle Ages, pacers were often much more expensive than ordinary horses.

teile.einleitung: The Iberian lynx is the smallest lynx in the world and lives only in Spain and Portugal. For a long time it was considered the most endangered cat species on Earth. Thanks to large conservation programmes, it has recovered remarkably well in recent years.
wichtigste: The Iberian lynx lives on the Iberian Peninsula, in Spain and Portugal.
It is the smallest lynx in the world.
For a long time it was considered the most endangered cat species in the world.
Its main food is wild rabbits.
Around 2002 there were fewer than 100 animals.
Thanks to breeding and release into the wild, over 2,000 Iberian lynxes live there again today (as of 2024).
In Switzerland, by contrast, the larger Eurasian lynx lives.

abschnitte.text: The Iberian lynx is called **Lynx pardinus** in science. It weighs about 9 to 15 kilograms, and males are heavier than females. Its yellowish-brown fur is covered with strong dark spots, a bit like a leopard's. Typical features are the **ear tufts** with black bunches of hair and a striking ruff of fur on the cheeks.

The Iberian lynx lives only on the **Iberian Peninsula** in the south-west of Europe. Most of the animals live in Andalusia, for example in the Sierra Morena and around Doñana National Park. Thanks to releases, there are now populations again in other parts of Spain and in Portugal. It likes a mix of scrubland, woods and open areas.

The Iberian lynx is a specialist, because **wild rabbits** make up by far the largest part of its food. A grown-up lynx needs roughly one rabbit a day. When diseases such as **myxomatosis** decimated the rabbits, the lynxes went hungry too. Now and then it also eats birds, mice or young deer.

Hunting, road building, the destruction of its habitat and a shortage of rabbits caused the population to fall sharply. Around the year 2002, fewer than 100 Iberian lynxes lived in the wild. At that time it was considered the most endangered cat species in the world. Many animals also died in **road accidents**.

Spain and Portugal started a large **breeding programme** and built breeding stations. Young lynxes were released in suitable areas, and rabbits were also resettled. By 2024 the population had grown to over 2,000 animals. As a result, in 2024 the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved the Iberian lynx down from endangered to **vulnerable**.

In Switzerland it is not the Iberian lynx that lives, but the larger **Eurasian lynx**. It had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1971. Today it roams through the Jura and the Alps and hunts mainly roe deer and chamois there. The two lynx species are closely related.

begriffe.erklaerung: The peninsula in the south-west of Europe that contains Spain and Portugal.
Ears with long tufts of hair at the tip, typical of lynxes.
Letting animals from breeding or care go out into nature.
A dangerous viral disease in rabbits.

gewusst: The Iberian lynx is the best-known example of how an almost extinct cat species can be saved.
In Spain, special tunnels were built under roads so that lynxes can safely cross beneath the carriageway.
An Iberian lynx is only about half as heavy as a large Eurasian lynx.

teile.einleitung: Pelicans are large waterbirds with a huge bill and a stretchable throat pouch beneath it. With it they catch fish like with a landing net. There are eight species of pelican worldwide, living on lakes, rivers and coasts.
wichtigste: The pelican family (Pelecanidae) includes eight species alive today.
Pelicans belong to the order Pelecaniformes.
Their closest relatives are the shoebill and the hamerkop.
The throat pouch of a large pelican holds about 11 litres of water.
The Australian pelican has the longest bill of all birds, at up to about 50 cm.
The Dalmatian pelican is the heaviest species, the brown pelican the smallest.
In pelicans, all four toes are joined by webbing.

abschnitte.text: Pelicans have a long neck, short legs and a very long bill with a **throat pouch** of stretchable skin. On their feet, all four toes are joined by **webbing**, so they paddle well. Under the skin and even into the bones they have many air sacs, which give them buoyancy in the water. In great heat they flutter the skin of the throat and throat pouch to cool down.

The **Dalmatian pelican** is regarded as the heaviest species and is one of the heaviest flying birds in the world. Its wings can reach a span of over three metres. The Australian pelican has the longest bill of all birds, at up to about 50 cm. The **brown pelican** from the Americas is the smallest of the eight species.

Pelicans eat mainly fish. Many species swim side by side in groups and drive fish into shallow water, where they scoop them out with their throat pouch. Then they let the water drain out at the sides and swallow the catch. The brown pelican, by contrast, plunges head first into the sea from the air to catch fish.

Pelicans live on every continent except Antarctica. In Europe the **great white pelican** and the Dalmatian pelican breed, mainly in south-eastern Europe, for example in the Danube Delta. Pelicans breed in colonies, often on islands or in reeds. In Switzerland you see pelicans almost only in zoos, or very rarely as lost visitors.

The name “pelican” comes from the ancient Greek word **pelekys**, which means “axe”, probably because of the shape of the bill. The Swedish naturalist Carl von Linné described the genus Pelecanus in 1758. Molecular studies show that the shoebill and the hamerkop are the closest relatives of the pelicans. Earlier, people thought that cormorants and gannets were their closest relatives.

Some pelican species are threatened by drained wetlands, disturbance at nesting sites and fishing nets. The Dalmatian pelican was rare in Europe for a long time, but its numbers are partly recovering thanks to **conservation projects**. In Christian art the pelican is an old symbol of self-sacrifice. According to a legend it is said to have fed its young with its own blood, which is not true.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stretchable pocket of skin under the bill with which pelicans catch fish.
Skin between the toes that acts like a paddle when swimming.
A large group of birds that breed close together.
The force that pushes something upwards in water and lets it float.

gewusst: A pelican's throat pouch holds more water than its stomach holds food.
Pelicans can soar for hours, almost without flapping their wings.
Pelicans have existed for a very long time, and fossils show that their bill has looked almost the same for millions of years.

teile.einleitung: Armoured catfish are small fish from South America whose bodies are covered with bony plates instead of scales. They root around on the bottom for food and eat scraps that other fish leave lying. That is why they are among the most popular fish in aquariums.
wichtigste: Armoured catfish come from the rivers and streams of South America.
Their body is armoured with two rows of bony plates.
They use their barbels to search for food on the bottom.
In an aquarium they eat leftover food, parts of plants and also some algae.
Armoured catfish can also swallow air and take in oxygen through the gut.
They like to live in groups and are peaceful fish.
The best known genus is called Corydoras.

abschnitte.text: Armoured catfish form the family **Callichthyidae** with over 200 species. Instead of scales they have two rows of **bony plates** on each side of the body, which protect them like armour. Around the mouth they have short threads, the **barbels**, which they use to feel and taste. Most species of the popular genus Corydoras grow to only 3 to 7 centimetres long.

Armoured catfish live in South America, for example in the **Amazon region**, in Brazil, Peru and Colombia. They inhabit calm rivers, streams and pools with a soft, sandy bottom. In the dry season the water can become warm and low in oxygen. They are well equipped for this with a special ability.

Besides gills, armoured catfish have a second way of breathing. They dart up to the surface in a flash, swallow air and take up the oxygen through the wall of their **gut**. This **gut breathing** helps them survive even in water that is low in oxygen. In an aquarium you can therefore see them dash briefly to the top now and then.

Armoured catfish root around in the sand with their barbels for small worms, insect larvae and other small animals. In an aquarium they eat leftovers that sink to the bottom, parts of plants and also some **algae**. That is why they are seen as useful helpers that keep the bottom clean. Even so, they need food of their own, for example special food tablets.

Armoured catfish are peaceful and well suited to **community tanks** with other calm fish. You should keep them in groups of at least six, because in nature they live in shoals. The bottom should be made of fine sand so that they do not hurt their sensitive barbels. Well-known species are the bronze corydoras and the panda corydoras with black patches around the eyes.

When mating, male and female often form a position that looks like a T. The female then carries a few eggs between her belly fins and sticks them to plants or to the aquarium glass. The parents do not look after the brood. After a few days tiny young fish hatch.

begriffe.erklaerung: Feeler-like threads around the mouth that fish use to feel and taste.
Taking in oxygen from swallowed air through the wall of the gut.
Hard plates made of bone that protect the body.
An aquarium in which different species of fish live together.

gewusst: Armoured catfish can wink an eye by briefly rotating it downwards.
Some armoured catfish have hard spines on their fins, which they can raise for protection.
In the Amazon, armoured catfish sometimes swim in shoals of hundreds of animals.

teile.einleitung: Pheromones are scent substances with which animals of the same species exchange messages. Ants use them to lay scent trails to food, and butterflies use them to attract a partner. Pheromones are a kind of chemical language that you do not hear but smell.
wichtigste: Pheromones are messenger substances for communication between animals of the same species.
Ants communicate mainly with scent substances and hardly at all with sounds.
Ants walk in lines because they follow the scent trail of another ant.
When an ant finds plenty of food, it calls many helpers with scent trails.
Many butterflies find their partner by giving off scent substances.
The term “pheromone” was introduced in 1959, among others by a Swiss researcher.
In agriculture, pheromones are used to protect plants.

abschnitte.text: Pheromones are chemical **messenger substances** that an animal gives off to influence other animals of its species. They often work even in tiny amounts. They are noticed with the sense of smell, in insects mostly with the **antennae**. The word is made up of Greek words and means roughly “to carry excitement”.

In social insects such as ants, pheromones are the most important language. When an ant finds food, it lays a **scent trail** on the way back to the nest. Other ants follow this trail and strengthen it for as long as there is food, which is why ants often walk in long lines. When an ant is attacked, it gives off an **alarm pheromone**, and its nestmates rush over or flee.

Many female moths give off a **sex attractant** to attract males. The males have large, feathered antennae and can detect the scent over long distances. The first pheromone to be studied exactly was bombykol of the silk moth, which the German chemist Adolf Butenandt described in 1959. For this he had to examine the scent glands of hundreds of thousands of females.

The word **pheromone** was proposed in 1959 by the German biochemist Peter Karlson and the Swiss insect researcher Martin Lüscher. Lüscher researched termites in particular and their scent substances. In honeybees, the queen controls life in the whole colony with her **queen substance**. Mammals such as cats, dogs and horses also react to pheromones, for example when marking territories.

In agriculture, **pheromone traps** are hung up to see when pests are flying. In Swiss winegrowing, the mating disruption method is often used: many small scent dispensers spread the attractant of the grape moth. The males then no longer find the females, and there are fewer caterpillars in the grapes. In this way, insecticide can be saved and beneficial insects spared.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scent substance with which animals of the same species communicate with each other.
A path of scent substances that other animals can follow.
A pheromone with which an animal attracts a partner.
A scent substance that warns members of the same species of danger.

gewusst: A male silk moth can detect a female's attractant when only a few molecules hit its antennae.
If you wipe a finger across an ant trail, the ants briefly lose the track.
Whether humans also have pheromones has still not been proven for certain.

teile.einleitung: Herbivores are animals that feed only, or almost only, on plants. They include large animals such as cows and elephants, but also small ones such as caterpillars and cockchafers. Because plants are hard to digest, herbivores often have special teeth and stomachs.
wichtigste: An animal that eats only plants is called a herbivore.
The technical term for this is herbivore.
The alpaca and the cockchafer are herbivores too.
Herbivores often have broad molar teeth for chewing.
Ruminants such as cows have a stomach with four sections.
In the food chain, herbivores are the food of many predators.

abschnitte.text: A **herbivore** feeds on grass, leaves, fruit, seeds, roots or nectar. Experts also say **herbivore** for this, from the Latin word “herba” meaning herb. By contrast, carnivores eat other animals, and omnivores eat both. Many herbivores specialise in particular parts of plants, such as seed eaters or fruit eaters.

Plants contain a lot of **cellulose**, a tough substance that animals find hard to digest. That is why herbivores have broad molar teeth, with which they grind their food thoroughly. In their gut, billions of bacteria help to break down the plants. Cows, sheep and goats are **ruminants**: they bring the food back up and chew it a second time.

In Switzerland, cows, sheep, goats and horses are well-known herbivores. In the wild, roe deer, red deer, ibex, chamois, marmots and brown hares live on plants. Many insects also eat plants, such as caterpillars, grasshoppers and the **cockchafer**, whose larvae even gnaw at roots. The alpaca from South America, which is also kept on Swiss farms, eats mainly grass and hay.

The largest land animals in the world, the **elephants**, are herbivores and eat over 100 kilograms of food a day. The koala eats almost only eucalyptus leaves, and the giant panda lives mainly on bamboo. Because plants provide little energy, many herbivores spend most of the day eating. Rabbits and hares even eat part of their own droppings to get more nutrients out.

abschnitte.titel: A place in the food chain
abschnitte.text: In the **food chain**, herbivores come directly after the plants. They turn plants into meat and are therefore prey for predators such as the wolf, lynx or fox. Many herbivores have eyes at the sides of the head so that they notice enemies early. They often live in herds, because many eyes see more and the individual is safer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A technical word for an animal that feeds on plants.
A herbivore that brings its food back up and chews it once more, like the cow.
The tough building material of plants, which is hard to digest.
The order of who eats whom, from the plants to the predators.

gewusst: A cow chews its cud for many hours every day, often while lying comfortably.
The giant panda belongs to the carnivores but eats almost only bamboo.
Many of the largest dinosaurs, such as the long-necked sauropods, were herbivores.
